title: Dispatch: detect stranded origin/<branch> from prior worker before creating a new worktree
description:
## Problem

When the forge re-dispatches a bead whose previous worker pushed commits to `origin/forge/<bead-id>` but never opened a PR, the new dispatch creates a fresh worktree from `main` and runs Smith from scratch. The fresh Smith produces a parallel implementation against the same bead description, then escalates on the inevitable non-fast-forward `git push`. The first attempt's pushed work, the second attempt's compute + Sonnet/Opus budget, and the operator's resolution time are all spent for nothing.

This is not a rare race. It fires every time a Smith escalates after `git push` but before `gh pr create` — a window that exists today because the pipeline's push and PR-open steps are not atomic and the orphan branch is not cleaned up on escalation.

### Concrete failure that motivated this bead

On 2026-05-18 the skybert-forge processed Fhi.Metadata-orjp2:

1. **Attempt 1** ran Smith on a clean worktree off `main` (`b04669d9f`). Produced two commits (`28c1d0751 feat: ...` + `e2083a4ae fix: prettier`), pushed to `origin/forge/Fhi.Metadata-orjp2`. Then escalated/crashed/timed-out between push and PR creation — `gh pr list --head forge/Fhi.Metadata-orjp2` returned `[]`.

2. **Attempt 2** dispatched on the next poll cycle. Created a fresh worktree from the same `b04669d9f` base — apparently without checking `origin/forge/Fhi.Metadata-orjp2` for prior content. Smith picked a different abstraction naming (`ListBackend` instead of `VariableListSource`) and added a higher-quality test/Share/Storybook layer, producing local commit `0ee25b36c`. Tried to push → non-fast-forward → escalated:

   > Smith escalated: origin/forge/Fhi.Metadata-orjp2 already has two commits from a prior worker ... My local commit 0ee25b36c is a parallel implementation ... A non-fast-forward git push is rejected; resolving this requires either force-pushing (discards the other worker's committed work) or resetting to origin (discards the additional tests/integration on top). Both are destructive operations beyond my authority.

The Smith escalation message is precise and human-friendly — but it fires at the END of a full worker run instead of at the START. Catching it at dispatch time avoids the wasted compute entirely.

## Root cause

The dispatch path checks for *local* worktree state (is there already a worktree directory for this bead?) but does not check the *remote* state (does `origin/forge/<bead-id>` already exist with commits beyond main?). When the prior worker's local worktree was cleaned up after escalation, the dispatch path sees a clean slate locally and proceeds — even though origin retains the partial work.

Likely files involved (verify before editing — names may have drifted):

- `internal/poller/` — the dispatch decision point.
- `internal/worktree/worktree.go` — `worktree.Create` does `git worktree add -B <branch> <path> origin/<branch>` when the ref exists. That call would actually pick up the prior commits if the dispatch path called it consistently — but the dispatch path may be passing a base that doesn't exist on origin yet (the bead is new) and falling back to creating from main.
- `internal/pipeline/pipeline.go` — pipeline orchestration; would need a pre-Schematic check to refuse to start if origin already has unmerged work.

## Proposed fix

**Step 1: pre-dispatch remote check.**

Before the dispatch path calls `worktree.Create`, run `git ls-remote origin forge/<bead-id>`. Outcomes:

- **No remote ref** → normal flow, dispatch as today.
- **Remote ref exists, is reachable from `origin/main`** → branch already merged; safe to delete the remote ref and proceed as normal. (`git push origin --delete forge/<bead-id>`).
- **Remote ref exists, is NOT reachable from `origin/main`** → prior attempt has unmerged work on origin. Do NOT dispatch. Instead:
  - Mark the bead as needs-attention with reason "prior worker pushed commits to `origin/forge/<bead-id>` but no PR was opened — needs human decision (accept, reset, or merge)".
  - Emit an event (`dispatch_blocked_stranded_branch` or similar).
  - Let Hearth 2.0 surface this via the resolve-needs-attention page from bead 07.

**Step 2: bonus — open PR atomically with push.**

The deeper bug is that `git push` and `gh pr create` are not atomic. If we open the PR *immediately* after a successful push (or if the push step is wrapped so that escalation between push and PR-create rolls the push back), the orphan-branch state stops existing and step 1's "no PR" case becomes unreachable.

The wrap-the-push option is fragile (rolling back a successful push is uncomfortable). The "open PR immediately, fail loud if it doesn't" option is cleaner. Today the Smith subprocess does the push; the PR creation may live in a later pipeline stage. If so, move it adjacent to the push so they share the same retry/escalation boundary.

**Step 3 (optional polish): branch staleness check on long-idle beads.**

For beads where the prior attempt completed normally (PR opened, then closed without merge), the `forge/<bead-id>` branch can sit on origin for a long time. A future dispatch on the same bead-id (e.g. via reopening the bead) would also collide. Mitigate by: when a PR for `forge/<bead-id>` is closed without merge, delete the branch as part of the close-handling logic in bellows.

## Acceptance criteria

- A bead that has been "push-but-no-PR" abandoned by a prior worker is NOT dispatched as a fresh worker on the next poll. Instead, it surfaces as needs-attention with a clear message in Hearth 2.0 (via bead 07's resolve UI when available; via the existing needs-attention surfaces in the meantime).
- A bead whose prior attempt's branch is already merged into main gets the stale branch cleaned up and is then dispatched normally.
- Smith subprocesses never see "your branch is behind origin/<branch>" / non-fast-forward errors as their FIRST signal that a prior attempt exists — the dispatch layer should catch this earlier.
- The fix is unit-testable with a fixture that pre-creates an `origin/forge/<bead-id>` ref pointing to a commit that's NOT reachable from main, then invokes the dispatch decision and asserts the bead is marked needs-attention rather than dispatched.
- For merged-and-stranded branches (rare but real), a fixture covering "origin/forge/<bead-id> is reachable from origin/main" passes via the cleanup path.
- An existing-PR check is preserved: if origin/<branch> exists AND a PR exists for it, the existing flow (bellows monitors the PR) continues unchanged. Dispatch should never duplicate a worker on a bead that already has a tracked PR.

## Notes / cross-refs

- Sister to bead 07 (Hearth 2.0 resolve-needs-attention UI). 07 makes resolving these escalations point-and-click; 08 makes them rare. Both are useful; neither blocks the other.
- The Smith's escalation message format from the 2026-05-18 Fhi.Metadata-orjp2 incident is excellent — preserve that text (or close to it) for the dispatch-time escalation reason so the operator's mental model is consistent regardless of when the check fires.
- Worker A's root cause for push-without-PR is unknown without pod logs. Hypotheses: (a) Smith timed out after push, before reaching `gh pr create`; (b) `gh pr create` hit transient auth/network failure and the pipeline didn't retry; (c) warden bounced post-push and the rollback path doesn't delete the branch. Worth surfacing in the daemon logs as a separate observability bead if it recurs.
- Multi-forge angle: if two forge instances share the same anvil, both could try to dispatch the same bead at different moments. The remote-check approach handles this naturally — whichever forge dispatches second sees the first's pushed branch and stays its hand. Without this fix, multi-forge deployments are even more exposed to the duplicate-work failure mode.
- Related to the spirit of bead 06 (reconcile clobber): both are "dispatch path doesn't consider all the relevant state before acting." This time it's remote git state instead of database state.
acceptance_criteria:
Test matrix:

- **No origin branch** → dispatch proceeds as today, Smith runs fresh.
- **Origin branch reachable from main** → branch deleted, dispatch proceeds. Subsequent `git ls-remote` returns empty.
- **Origin branch NOT reachable from main, no PR exists** → bead marked needs-attention with descriptive reason; no Smith dispatched; event logged.
- **Origin branch exists AND PR exists** → no duplicate dispatch; existing bellows monitor continues.
- **`git ls-remote` network failure** → dispatch proceeds (fail open); Smith's push-time check remains the safety net.
- **Multi-forge race**: two forges polling the same bead within the same poll cycle; whichever pushes first wins, the other sees the remote branch and skips.
- **Re-dispatch after operator resolves**: once a human runs `forge queue clear <bead-id>` AND the stale branch is gone (either merged or manually deleted), dispatch proceeds normally on the next poll.
notes:
See bead 07 for the operator-facing resolution UI. Implementing 08 without 07 is fine — needs-attention beads already surface in the existing Events panel; 07 just adds point-and-click resolution.

The deeper push-then-PR atomicity problem (the secondary fix in "Step 2") is also worth a separate, smaller bead if you don't want to bundle it. Recommend bundling: it's tightly coupled (the dispatch-time check exists *because* push and PR-open aren't atomic) and the diff is small.

Multi-forge note: this bead becomes more valuable as the forge fleet grows. With one forge per anvil today, the duplicate-work failure mode mostly fires across retry attempts of the same forge. With multiple forges per anvil (which the per-instance marker work from earlier already enables), it would fire across forges too. Worth landing before that path of expansion gets used heavily.

title: Hearth 2.0: add a resolve-needs-attention page for escalated beads / workers
description:
## Problem

Hearth 2.0 (the React web UI at /forge) surfaces escalated beads and failed workers in the Workers + Events panels but does NOT offer any in-UI mechanism to resolve them. The user has to drop to a pod shell and invoke the forge CLI by hand (`forge queue clarify|unclarify|retry|clear|stop`) to clear flags and re-dispatch. The original Hearth TUI (`forge ledger` / `forge hearth`) has interactive resolution built in.

When forge runs locally on a developer's laptop, the workflow gap is tolerable — they `forge ledger` in another terminal. When forge runs in a pod (skybert, hetzner), it forces an extra `kubectl exec` per resolution. Combined with multi-worker dispatch contention, escalations happen frequently enough that the gap is a real ergonomic and ops-velocity cost.

### Concrete failure that motivated this bead

On 2026-05-18 the skybert-forge dispatched Fhi.Metadata-orjp2 twice. Worker A pushed `origin/forge/Fhi.Metadata-orjp2` with two commits but never opened a PR and escalated. Worker B was re-dispatched from the same base commit, made a parallel implementation with different abstraction naming + tests + ShareModal/story integration, then escalated on non-fast-forward push:

> Dispatch attempt 2 failed for Fhi.Metadata-orjp2: Smith escalated: origin/forge/Fhi.Metadata-orjp2 already has two commits from a prior worker ... My local commit 0ee25b36c is a parallel implementation ... A non-fast-forward git push is rejected; resolving this requires either force-pushing (discards the other worker's committed work) or resetting to origin (discards the additional tests/integration on top). Both are destructive operations beyond my authority.

The escalation message is itself excellent — it lists the exact commits, the exact local branch tip, the trade-off, and frames the human decision needed. The UI just needs a place to act on it.

## What "resolve" needs to do

When a bead or worker is in needs-attention state, the user needs (at minimum) to be able to:

- **See the escalation message** in full (today it's clamped/scrolled in the Events panel).
- **See related context**: which commits exist on `origin/<branch>`, which exist locally (in the pod worktree), the diff range, the parent base.
- **Choose a resolution path** from a small set of pre-defined actions, with confirmation:
  - "Accept origin / clear flag" — equivalent to `forge queue clear <id>`. Use when origin already has acceptable code and the worker can stop trying.
  - "Reset & retry" — equivalent to `forge queue retry <id>`. Resets retry counter and re-dispatches on next poll. Use when the failure was transient.
  - "Mark needs clarification" / "Unmark" — equivalent to `forge queue clarify|unclarify <id>`. Use when the bead description needs more info before the work can complete.
  - "Stop worker" — equivalent to `forge queue stop <id> --anvil <name>`. Use when a worker is hung or doing the wrong thing.
  - "Open PR manually" — links out to `gh pr create` flow (or a small in-UI form). Use when origin has the work but no PR was opened.
- **Add a comment / note** that gets logged to the bead's event stream (audit trail of "why we resolved it this way").

## Where this lives in Hearth 2.0

Probably either:

1. A new dedicated route `/forge/escalations` listing all current needs-attention items across all anvils, with per-row action buttons.
2. An expandable detail panel on the existing Workers/PR panel that opens when you click on a needs-attention row — the actions live inside the panel.

Option 2 is closer to how the original Hearth TUI works (you select a row in the ledger and hit a key for the action) and probably preserves the existing layout better. Option 1 makes the escalations more findable as a category. The implementer should pick — both are reasonable.

Looking at the existing `internal/web/forge_chat.go` + `internal/web/views.go` plus the React side, the precedent for "interactive action on a server-side row" already exists (`assign_bellows`, `approve`, `rebase` actions via pr_action IPC). The new actions can follow the same IPC-action pattern: HTTP POST from the UI → IPC `queue_action` (or per-action `queue_clear`, `queue_retry`, etc) → daemon handler updates state.db + emits an event for the audit trail.

## Acceptance criteria

- A user viewing Hearth 2.0 in a browser can resolve a `dispatch_failed` / `smith_failed` / `needs_human` escalation without dropping to a shell.
- The five CLI verbs (`clear`, `retry`, `clarify`, `unclarify`, `stop`) are reachable from the UI with confirmation prompts on the destructive ones (`stop`, `retry`).
- Each resolution writes an event to the `events` table so there is an audit trail.
- The full escalation message is readable (no truncation in the resolve flow even if the events panel clamps it for the overview).
- Works for both bead-level escalations (e.g. dispatch_failed) and worker-level escalations (e.g. smith_failed).
- Multi-forge safe: when two forges share the same Dolt-backed bead view, the action is scoped to the forge that owns the worker (forge_id check) and rejects with a clear message if a different forge owns it.

## Notes / cross-refs

- Original Hearth TUI: `forge hearth` (bubbletea) + `forge ledger` (interactive bead management). The action shortcuts there are the spec for what we want available in Hearth 2.0.
- CLI verbs documented in `Forge/CLAUDE.md` Quick Reference: queue clarify|unclarify|retry|clear|stop.
- IPC pattern reference: `internal/daemon/daemon.go:4656` (assign_bellows handler) is a good template — short async handler that updates state.db and emits an event.
- Hearth 2.0 dist: `internal/web/dist/` — rebuilt frontend lives here. Plan: React route + a small Zustand/Redux slice for in-flight resolution requests, talking to a new `/api/forge/resolve` endpoint that bridges to the daemon IPC.
- When this lands, the Fhi.Metadata-orjp2 collision class becomes a 30-second point-and-click instead of the 10-minute shell-and-diff investigation it was today.
design:
Implementation outline (tune as you go — these are pointers, not a frozen plan):

1. **Backend endpoint**. Add `POST /api/forge/queue/<verb>` for verb in {clear, retry, clarify, unclarify, stop}, plus optional `POST /api/forge/queue/note` for adding an event-stream comment. Each endpoint:
   - Accepts JSON body with `{bead_id: string, anvil?: string, reason?: string}`.
   - Calls into the daemon via the existing IPC socket (newline-delimited JSON, see internal/ipc/ipc.go).
   - Returns 200 + the updated row JSON on success, 4xx with a clear error on auth/scope/forge_id mismatch.

2. **Daemon-side handlers**. In `internal/daemon/daemon.go`, add IPC cases mirroring the existing `assign_bellows` / `approve` / `rebase` pattern. Each handler:
   - Validates the bead/worker is owned by THIS forge (forge_id check).
   - Performs the corresponding state.db update.
   - Logs an event with EventType like `queue_cleared`, `queue_retry_requested`, etc., with the user-supplied reason in the message.
   - For `retry`, also resets the retry counter and lets the next poller iteration re-dispatch.
   - For `stop`, sends the kill signal to the worker subprocess via the existing kill_worker IPC path.

3. **Frontend route + component**. Either:
   - New `/forge/escalations` route: lists all `workers WHERE needs_attention=1 OR status=stalled` with a "Resolve" button per row that opens a modal with the action buttons.
   - OR a detail panel on the existing Workers/PR row click that includes the same action buttons inline. (Lighter touch, recommended.)
   - Use shadcn/ui primitives consistent with the rest of Hearth 2.0.

4. **Audit trail**. The `events` table already takes a `message` column — repurpose it. UI should display the audit trail filtered by bead_id when the resolve modal is open, so the operator can see "ah, the prior attempt was cleared with reason X" before deciding.

5. **Multi-forge safety**. The forge_id check is the new column added in bead 06 (`bellows_manually_assigned`-style). The handlers should refuse to act on workers that don't belong to this forge instance, returning a clear "this worker belongs to forge <other-id> — log into that forge's Hearth to resolve" error.

6. **Tests**. Daemon-level unit tests for each handler (smithy-fail fixture, dispatch-fail fixture). React-side component test for the resolve modal (mock the API).

Do NOT include force-push or fast-forward-reset actions in the UI. Those are intentionally CLI-only — the operator should never have a 1-click "discard the other worker's committed code" button. If a destructive git operation is genuinely needed, it stays a manual `git push --force` from a shell, with the operator explicitly opting in.
acceptance_criteria:
See main Problem section. Concrete test scenarios:

- A bead with status=needs_attention shows up in the new resolve flow and can be cleared in 2 clicks.
- Clicking "Reset & retry" triggers a re-dispatch within one poll cycle and emits a queue_retry_requested event.
- Clicking "Stop worker" on a running worker terminates the subprocess and transitions the row to status=stopped.
- A multi-forge scenario where two forges share a Dolt bead view: forge A's Hearth refuses to resolve a worker that belongs to forge B and explains why.
- The full escalation message text is visible in the resolve modal (no truncation), independent of how the Events panel summarizes it.
notes:
Discovered while resolving a real dispatch_failed for Fhi.Metadata-orjp2 on skybert-forge on 2026-05-18. The investigation + decision + execution took ~10 minutes of kubectl-exec / git-log / forge-CLI work; with a resolve page it would have been seconds.

Sister to bead 04 / 05 / 06 (bellows polish), but on the Hearth-2.0-UX side rather than the bellows-state-machine side. Doesn't depend on those landing first.

Original Hearth TUI (`forge hearth` / `forge ledger`) is the spec to mirror — read those skill flows before designing the new UI surface so the verbs and confirmations match.

title: Temper: cap Vitest worker concurrency to reduce smith-OOM kills
description:
On a memory-constrained host, Forge's Temper stage runs Vitest with default worker concurrency (≈ N CPU cores worth of workers). Each worker can use 1+ GB of RSS on Vite-based frontends, and the smith subprocess + Vite/dev tooling + Hytte web service together routinely push the box past its 7.6 GB RAM, triggering OOM kills.

Real example today: a smith was working on Hytte-i9tm (Pokémon CardScanner). Two Vitest worker processes hit 4.3 GB and 2.0 GB RSS respectively, on top of the smith's own 4 GB. The kernel OOM-killed the smith THREE times in one hour. Adding swap mitigated the immediate damage but the underlying cost of Temper running uncapped Vitest workers is still there.

## Fix

In `internal/temper/` (or wherever the auto-detected Vitest step is built — likely `internal/temper/node.go` or similar that detects `package.json`), append worker-capping arguments when invoking Vitest:

    vitest run --pool=threads --poolOptions.threads.maxThreads=1 --poolOptions.threads.minThreads=1

(Or use `--maxWorkers=1` if that's the supported flag for the detected version.)

Concretely:
- If the package's package.json has `"test": "vitest ..."` and Temper rewrites/wraps it, append the concurrency flags.
- If Temper uses its own `vitest run` command, just include the flags there.
- Make this configurable via the existing per-anvil Temper config (`temper.commands` / `temper.steps`) so a user can opt out by overriding the command. Default behaviour: single-threaded.

Don't add the flags universally to `go test` or other runners — they don't have this issue.

## Optional: env-based opt-out

A small `temper.vitest_max_threads` config knob (default 1, can be set higher if the user knows their host can take it). Defer if it adds friction; the single-threaded default is fine for the Hetzner box.

## Tests

Add a unit test in `internal/temper/` that, given a sample Node project with a vitest test step, asserts the constructed command line includes the maxThreads cap.

## Acceptance

- `make build`, `make test`, `go vet ./...` pass.
- A smith finishing on a Vitest-heavy bead no longer triggers OOM kills on the Hetzner box (observable via `dmesg | grep oom`).
- Existing Vitest tests still pass — single-thread mode is slower but functionally identical.
- Per-anvil override still works.
- Changelog fragment in changelog.d/ (category: Fixed).

## Reference

- internal/temper/ — auto-detection logic for Node/Vitest.
- Today's OOM evidence in `journalctl -k`:

      Out of memory: Killed process 763882 (MainThread) total-vm:34522188kB, anon-rss:4311428kB ... task_memcg=/system.slice/forge.service

- Vitest workers docs: https://vitest.dev/config/#poolOptions.

## Non-goals

- Disabling Vitest in Temper entirely. CI handles the comprehensive test pass; Temper is a smoke gate.
- Memory limits on the smith subprocess itself.
- Migrating away from Vitest.

## Future-option (option X from the discussion)

If even single-threaded Vitest is too heavy on this host, the next step is to **skip frontend tests in Temper and rely solely on CI** for the test signal. Document this as the next escalation if (a) Temper Vitest still triggers OOMs after the worker cap, or (b) Temper Vitest meaningfully extends the smith pipeline duration. Not implemented in this bead.

title: Bellows does not re-emit EventReviewChanges when unresolved threads persist across review-fix cycles
description:
## Problem

After the first burnish (review-fix) cycle completes on a PR, any subsequent unresolved review threads on the same PR never trigger another burnish — bellows sees no transition and silently sits there. The PR is open and non-mergeable but bellows is effectively asleep.

Observed on skybert-forge today (2026-05-13) for ext-3082 (the still-open companion to ext-3073 from bead 04): quench fixed the initial CI failures, then the reviewer left new review comments. The bellows worker `bellows-munin-3082` is in `monitoring` (correct), Hearth shows the PR with unresolved threads, but no burnish ever spawns. The PR sits with `prs.status=open` and the threads stay unresolved indefinitely.

## Root cause

`internal/bellows/bellows.go` has asymmetric transition coverage between CI fixes and review fixes:

**CI flow (line 538-585)** has *three* branches:
1. `newSnap.CIPassing && !lastSnap.CIPassing` → emit EventCIPassed.
2. `!newSnap.CIPassing && !ciInProgress && lastSnap.CIPassing` → emit EventCIFailed (first failure).
3. `!newSnap.CIPassing && !ciInProgress && !lastSnap.CIPassing` → still-failing branch: re-emit EventCIFailed if `pr.Status != PRNeedsFix && pr.CIFixCount > 0 && pr.CIFixCount < maxCI`. This is the branch that keeps the retry loop alive across multiple quench attempts.

**Review flow (line 619-636)** has *one* branch:
1. `(newSnap.NeedsChanges && !lastSnap.NeedsChanges) || (newSnap.HasUnresolvedThreads && !lastSnap.HasUnresolvedThreads)` → emit EventReviewChanges.

No equivalent of the still-failing branch. Combined with the seeding guard at line 408-412:
```go
threadsSeed := pr.HasUnresolvedThreads
if threadsSeed && pr.Status != state.PRNeedsFix && pr.ReviewFixCount == 0 {
    threadsSeed = false
}
```
this is what happens after the first burnish:
- Daemon calls `NotifyReviewFixCompleted` → DB row flips `prs.status: needs_fix → open` (via `UpdatePRStatusIfNeedsFix` in `internal/lifecycle/lifecycle.go:499`).
- Daemon calls `ResetPRState` → snapshot cache wiped.
- Reviewer leaves new comments. `prs.has_unresolved_threads` is true.
- Next bellows poll: `pr.ReviewFixCount=1`, so the seeding guard does NOT clear threadsSeed. `lastSnap.HasUnresolvedThreads=true`.
- `newSnap.HasUnresolvedThreads=true`.
- Transition test `(new && !last)` evaluates to `(true && !true) = false`. No event emitted. No burnish.

The seeding guard's `ReviewFixCount == 0` clause is deliberate — once a burnish has run, the guard refuses to pretend threads were absent. But the missing still-failing branch means there is now no path to ever fire EventReviewChanges again until threads transition from 0 back to N+. Reviewers don't usually resolve all threads and then re-add comments; they add to the existing pile. So in practice the bead is stuck.

The CI-path equivalent of this guard plus the still-failing branch is the entire reason that loop keeps working — burnish needs the mirror.

## Proposed fix

Mechanical: add a parallel "still has unresolved threads" branch in `checkPR`, immediately after the existing review-fix block at line 619-636 (using `else if` against the existing condition so the two are mutually exclusive — matches the CI pattern). Pseudo-diff:

```go
// existing block at 619-636 (unchanged)
if (newSnap.NeedsChanges && !lastSnap.NeedsChanges) || (newSnap.HasUnresolvedThreads && !lastSnap.HasUnresolvedThreads) {
    // ...emit EventReviewChanges, set PRNeedsFix...
} else if newSnap.HasUnresolvedThreads && lastSnap.HasUnresolvedThreads {
    // Review still has unresolved threads with no transition. Catches the gap
    // where NotifyReviewFixCompleted() resets pr.Status to open after a burnish
    // cycle but bellows never re-emits EventReviewChanges because threads stayed
    // > 0 across the cycle. Mirrors the CI-fix still-failing branch above.
    maxR := m.maxReviewFixAttempts()
    if pr.Status != state.PRNeedsFix && pr.ReviewFixCount > 0 && pr.ReviewFixCount < maxR {
        m.emit(ctx, PREvent{
            PRNumber:  pr.Number,
            BeadID:    pr.BeadID,
            Anvil:     pr.Anvil,
            Branch:    status.HeadRefName,
            EventType: EventReviewChanges,
            Details:   fmt.Sprintf("PR still has unresolved review threads after fix attempt %d/%d", pr.ReviewFixCount, maxR),
            Timestamp: time.Now(),
        })
        _ = m.db.UpdatePRStatus(pr.ID, state.PRNeedsFix)
        _ = m.db.LogEvent(state.EventReviewChanges, fmt.Sprintf("PR #%d review fix retry needed (attempt %d/%d)", pr.Number, pr.ReviewFixCount, maxR), pr.BeadID, pr.Anvil)
        _ = m.db.LogEvent(state.EventPRNeedsFix, fmt.Sprintf("PR #%d review fix retry needed", pr.Number), pr.BeadID, pr.Anvil)
    }
}
```

Guards (mirror of CI path):
- `pr.Status != state.PRNeedsFix` — only re-emit if the PR is currently *not* in a fix cycle. Prevents firing during an in-flight burnish.
- `pr.ReviewFixCount > 0` — only after at least one attempt completed (i.e. only relevant in the post-first-fix state where the seeding guard refuses to clear `threadsSeed`).
- `pr.ReviewFixCount < maxR` — respect the configured cap so runaway retries are still blocked. Likely `m.maxReviewFixAttempts()` already exists; confirm the helper name in this file.

A cleaner alternative would be to also re-emit when `(NewUnresolvedCount > LastUnresolvedCount)`, but bellows tracks bool not int. Counting is out of scope; the still-failing branch is sufficient.

## Acceptance

- A PR that's already had one completed burnish cycle and now has new unresolved threads triggers a fresh burnish within one bellows poll, as long as `pr.ReviewFixCount < max_review_fix_attempts`.
- The retry cap is respected: when `pr.ReviewFixCount == max_review_fix_attempts`, no re-emit fires (existing `needs_human` flow takes over).
- An in-flight burnish (`pr.Status == PRNeedsFix`) does NOT receive duplicate dispatches from this branch.
- A PR whose threads are still genuinely 0 (never had review changes) is unaffected — the branch only fires when `lastSnap.HasUnresolvedThreads && newSnap.HasUnresolvedThreads`.
- Unit test mirroring the CI still-failing test exists for this branch.
- Manual end-to-end: assign bellows to an external PR with CI failures + review comments, run quench to green, push a new commented review, observe burnish dispatching within one poll.

## Notes

Sister bug to bead 04 (`04-bellows-cleanup-external-prs.sh`) — both are transition-detection gaps in bellows. 04 is the cleanup-after-terminal gap (worker rows orphaned in `monitoring`); this one is the retry-after-fix gap (burnish never re-fires).

The symptom is identical from the user's perspective ("bellows isn't doing anything") but the failures occur on opposite sides of the PR lifecycle: 04 is post-merge/close, 05 is mid-flight. They should be fixed independently; do not bundle them in one PR.

When building the unit test, the existing CI still-failing test (search for `CIFixCount.*maxCI` in `internal/bellows/bellows_test.go` if it exists, otherwise nearest equivalent) is the template — set up two consecutive polls with both snapshots having unresolved threads, advance the PR row to `pr.ReviewFixCount=1`, assert EventReviewChanges fires on the second poll.

File of interest: `internal/bellows/bellows.go:619-636` (the existing one-branch review block) and `internal/bellows/bellows.go:564-585` (the CI still-failing template). Likely also touches `bellows_test.go`.

The whole forge has been hammering away just fine on CI failures, but it turns out review comments slip right through the cracks like a dropped nail.
design:
See main Problem section for the diff sketch. Key design points:

1. **Why `else if`, not `if`** — matches CI pattern, makes the two branches mutually exclusive, and avoids double-emitting in the rare case where both `(0→N) NEW threads` and `pr.ReviewFixCount > 0` are true simultaneously (which would mean a daemon restart mid-cycle landed the snapshot in an inconsistent state — vanishingly unlikely but still cheaper to avoid).
2. **Why gate on `pr.Status != PRNeedsFix`** — prevents firing during an active burnish. Without this guard, every poll cycle during a burnish run would re-emit and re-dispatch, racing the existing worker.
3. **Why `ReviewFixCount > 0` not `>= 0`** — the initial 0→N transition is covered by the existing branch. Adding `>= 0` would make this branch fire for first-time threads too, which is benign but redundant.
4. **Why the seeding guard at line 410 still belongs** — it's the only thing keeping the first-time transition correct across daemon restarts (PR was already at unresolved=true when daemon came up; without the guard, lastSnap=true and newSnap=true, no transition). Don't remove or weaken it as part of this fix.
5. **maxReviewFixAttempts** — verify the accessor name on `Monitor` before pasting. The CI path uses `m.maxCIFixAttempts()` (line 571), so the review counterpart is likely `m.maxReviewFixAttempts()`. If it doesn't exist, add it as a thin wrapper mirroring the CI one.

Do NOT also touch the seeding guard's `ReviewFixCount == 0` clause. It is correct as-is — its job is to handle daemon-restart-with-stale-threads, not the post-fix retry case (which is exactly what this new branch is for).
acceptance_criteria:
See main Problem section. Test matrix:
- Post-fix retry: poll1=(threads=true, RFC=0), poll2=(threads=true, RFC=1, status=open) → expect EventReviewChanges on poll2.
- Cap respected: poll with `RFC=max_review_fix_attempts` → no emit.
- In-flight: poll with `pr.Status=PRNeedsFix` → no emit.
- Genuinely no threads: poll1=(threads=false), poll2=(threads=false) → no emit.
- First transition still works: poll1=(threads=false), poll2=(threads=true) → existing branch fires, new branch does not.
notes:
Sister to bead 04. Same bellows-transition-gap family of bug, opposite end of the PR lifecycle. Treating as priority 2 because it strands the most useful bellows feature (auto-fix review comments on external PRs the user has assigned) and the workaround (manually delete + re-add bellows assignment to force re-seed) is annoying.

When this is fixed, ext-3082 should self-recover on the next bellows poll without any manual nudge.

title: Bellows leaves monitoring worker for closed external PR after bellows_managed flip
description:
## Problem

When a user manually assigns bellows to an external PR (`ext-*`, `bellows_managed=1`) and the PR later closes or merges on GitHub, the bellows worker row in `state.db` stays in `monitoring` indefinitely. Hearth 2.0 keeps surfacing it under Workers even though the underlying PR is terminal.

Concrete: on skybert-forge today (2026-05-13) the worker `bellows-munin-3073` for ext-3073 was still `monitoring` after the user closed PR #3073 on GitHub. The companion ext-3082 worker (still open) was correctly active. After manual cleanup
```sql
UPDATE workers SET status='done', completed_at='2026-05-13T06:59:48.765714Z' WHERE id='bellows-munin-3073';
```
the panel cleared. By contrast, Forge-created PRs (`bellows_managed=1` from creation) transition cleanly via `CompleteWorkersByBead(pr.BeadID)` inside `checkPR` — the bug is specific to ext-* PRs that flip from unmanaged → managed.

## Root cause

In `internal/bellows/bellows.go` the two relevant code paths are:

1. **Unmanaged ext-* early-return** (around line 456-465 in `checkPR`): for `ext-* && !bellows_managed`, the function persists merged/closed status unconditionally and returns. So an ext-* PR can be sitting at `prs.status=merged` or `prs.status=closed` in our DB *before* the user clicks "assign bellows".
2. **Managed terminal-detection branches** (around lines 476 and 517 in `checkPR`): the `IsMerged && pr.Status != PRMerged` and `IsClosed && pr.Status != PRClosed` branches are the ones that call `CompleteWorkersByBead(pr.BeadID)`. They are gated on `pr.Status` not already being terminal.
3. **`OpenPRs()` filter** (`internal/state/db.go:1035`): only returns PRs whose status is non-terminal. So once the PR is at `prs.status=merged|closed`, it falls out of the poll set entirely.

Sequence that produces the bug:
- ext-3073 exists with `bellows_managed=0`, `status=open`.
- User merges/closes the PR on GitHub.
- One bellows poll cycle later, the unmanaged-path early-return persists `prs.status=closed`.
- User now flips `bellows_managed=1` (via the assign-bellows IPC/API). A worker row `bellows-munin-3073` is created with `status=monitoring`.
- From this point on `OpenPRs()` never returns ext-3073 again, so `checkPR` never runs for it, so the managed terminal-detection branches never fire, so `CompleteWorkersByBead` is never called. The worker row is orphaned in `monitoring`.

The same bug can also happen in the reverse order if the assignment happened first AND the close fired between two polls AND the cached `lastStatuses` was wiped (e.g. daemon restart): the snapshot seeding can mask the open→closed transition. The dominant scenario is the one above, however.

## Proposed fix

One or both of the following — option A is the smaller, more surgical fix and is the recommended path:

**Option A (preferred): orphan-worker sweep in bellows.**

At the start of each `checkAll` poll (or as a sibling pass in `Run`), enumerate workers where `phase='bellows'` and `status='monitoring'`, and for each one look up the corresponding PR row. If the PR is in a terminal status (`merged`, `closed`) — or has no matching PR row at all — call `db.UpdateWorkerStatus(workerID, WorkerDone)` with `completed_at=now`. Net add: ~15 lines in `internal/bellows/bellows.go` plus a helper on `state.DB` to enumerate monitoring bellows workers.

**Option B (complementary): close the race on bellows assignment.**

In the IPC handler that flips `bellows_managed=0 → 1` (find via `grep -rn "bellows_managed" cmd/ internal/`), check the persisted `prs.status` and refuse to create a `monitoring` worker if the PR is already in a terminal state — or proactively call the terminal-branch logic (event emit + ingot update + no worker insert). This prevents the orphan from being created in the first place.

A also catches any *other* path that could leave a bellows worker stranded (e.g. a future bug, a manual SQL tweak, a daemon-restart-mid-merge scenario), so it is the safer long-term fix.

## Acceptance

- Manually creating the buggy state and running one bellows poll cycle transitions the orphaned worker to `done`:
  1. With Forge running, create or pick an `ext-*` PR row, set `bellows_managed=0`.
  2. Close it on GitHub.
  3. After the next bellows poll, confirm `prs.status=closed` (or `=merged`).
  4. Set `bellows_managed=1` for that row and insert a `bellows-<anvil>-<num>` worker with `status=monitoring` (mimics the IPC flip path).
  5. Within one bellows poll cycle, the worker should transition to `status=done` with `completed_at` set.
- The Hearth 2.0 Workers panel no longer shows bellows entries for terminal-state external PRs.
- `CompletedWorkers` returns the swept worker so it appears in history rather than just disappearing.
- Forge-managed (`bellows-managed=1` since creation) PRs continue to follow the existing `CompleteWorkersByBead` path — no regression there.
- A unit test covers the orphan-sweep path: insert a bellows monitoring worker whose PR is in `merged` status, run one pass of the sweep, assert worker is `done`.
acceptance_criteria:
See main Problem section. Key checks:
- Orphaned `monitoring` bellows worker for a terminal-state PR is swept to `done` within one bellows poll.
- Hearth 2.0 Workers panel no longer surfaces bellows for closed/merged external PRs.
- Forge-managed bellows worker lifecycle is unchanged (no false sweeps mid-flight — sweep only catches `monitoring` rows whose PR is *already* terminal).
- Unit test covers the sweep against a fixture DB.
notes:
Discovered on skybert-forge while testing bellows on two external PRs (ext-3082 still open, ext-3073 closed by user). Worker `bellows-munin-3073` was stuck `monitoring` and Hearth 2.0 kept rendering it. Cleaned up by direct UPDATE on `~/.forge/state.db` in the pod (already done as of 2026-05-13 06:59 UTC). This bead is for the persistent fix.

Related context the implementer might want:
- `internal/bellows/bellows.go` lines 270-326 = `checkAll` upsert loop (skips unmanaged ext-*).
- `internal/bellows/bellows.go` lines 329-536 = `checkPR` with the unmanaged early-return at 456 and the managed terminal branches at 476/517.
- `internal/bellows/bellows.go` lines 218-270 = `reconcileTerminalStates` — runs once at startup over `OpenPRs()` filtered to `PRNeedsFix`. NOT a general sweep, so not the right place for the fix on its own.
- `internal/state/db.go:799` = `CompleteWorkersByBead` — matches by `bead_id` column, status IN (pending,running,reviewing,monitoring,stalled).
- `internal/state/db.go:1035` = `OpenPRs` — filters out terminal statuses, which is the trap.

The puzzle is solved; the worker was just hammering at the door long after the PR had hung up its tools.

title: Beads-Forge over-splits simple tasks into multiple sequential beads
description:
## Problem

The Beads-Forge final stage emits multiple sequential beads for work that is plainly a single self-contained task. Concrete example from today: a react-day-picker v9→v10 dependency upgrade on the munin client produced FOUR beads:

- Fhi.Metadata-lenyo — Audit react-day-picker usage in munin client
- Fhi.Metadata-xmrma — Bump react-day-picker to ^10.0.0 and resolve peer deps
- Fhi.Metadata-5hziz — Migrate munin client source to react-day-picker v10 API
- Fhi.Metadata-2kogb — Update tests and perform visual QA for react-day-picker v10

This is one PR's worth of work that any human dev would do in one sitting, in one branch, against one reviewer. Splitting it produces:
- Artificial sequencing overhead (each bead has its own Smith → Temper → Warden → PR cycle).
- Multi-PR chains that are harder to review than a single coherent diff.
- Worker thrash: temper has to re-run npm install/build at every step.
- A trail of beads to close by hand when the human collapses them back into one PR anyway.

All four beads were closed and replaced with a single Fhi.Metadata-fel9j covering the whole upgrade.

## Proposed fix

Retune the prompt that decides whether to emit one bead vs many in the Beads-Forge \"grilling → ready → create\" transition. Default to ONE bead unless the work crosses meaningful boundaries — see Design below for the heuristic. The current behaviour appears to be \"if you can list more than one phase, split it,\" which produces a bead per Verb (\"audit\", \"migrate\", \"test\") instead of per Deliverable.
design:
Likely lives in the Beads-Forge emission prompt — probably `internal/web/forge_emit.go` or the prompt assembled in the chat runner for the create-beads stage. Verify.

Proposed heuristic for the prompt (paraphrase, tune as needed):

> Emit ONE bead unless the work meets at least one of these split criteria:
> - It spans multiple anvils.
> - It requires changes in two or more independent code areas (e.g. API + client) that ship as separate PRs in your team's workflow.
> - One slice of the work is genuinely blocked on another's merge (e.g. needs an interface migration to land first).
> - The work is large enough that a single PR would be unreviewable (>500 lines of net diff across >10 files is a rough threshold).
>
> A dependency upgrade, a single new feature in one package, a bug fix, or a refactor inside one module is ONE bead — even if the work has phases like \"audit, change, test\". Those are stages of one piece of work, not separate deliverables.

The over-splitting failure is symmetric with the under-splitting failure: be willing to single-bead aggressively and let the human flag if it should have been split. A single bead that turns out to be too big is easier to chunk after the fact (decompose via Schematic) than four beads that turn out to be one is to consolidate.
acceptance_criteria:
- A drafting session for a single-PR dependency upgrade (e.g. \"bump react-day-picker to v10\") produces exactly one bead.
- A bug fix to one file produces exactly one bead.
- A genuinely multi-area feature (e.g. \"Explorer auth: cookie scheme + OIDC scheme + policy\" or a new backend endpoint + frontend component pair) still splits appropriately.
- The prompt change is captured as a comment in the code explaining the heuristic so the next round of tuning knows what was intentionally rejected.
notes: See the closed beads Fhi.Metadata-{lenyo,xmrma,5hziz,2kogb} for the canonical over-split example. The replacement single bead is Fhi.Metadata-fel9j. Pair this fix with the drafting-agent filesystem-access bead — that one removes the trivial-question failure mode that often pushes the splitting decision into \"better split it just in case\" territory.

title: Beads-Forge drafting agent: give it filesystem access and resolve anvil path from bead metadata
description:
## Problem

When drafting a new bead in Hearth 2.0's Beads-Forge UI, the drafting agent claims it can't read the codebase yet (\"in this drafting stage I'm working without filesystem access\") and falls back to asking trivial design questions whose answers are sitting in the repo. Worse, it then asks the user for the filesystem path of the anvil — even though the anvil is already chosen on the page and the path is known to Forge from `forge.yaml`.

Observed during today's react-day-picker v9→v10 draft:
- \"if you want to move straight to a concrete plan, just say the word and I'll start digging through the codebase\" — drafting flow shouldn't require user permission to grep.
- \"Where is the munin client codebase located? I need filesystem access to audit actual react-day-picker usage\" — the bead already targets the munin anvil; the path is `anvils.munin.path` in the daemon's config.
- Two consecutive questions both blocked on the same path the agent already had access to derive.

## Proposed fix

Two independent improvements to the drafting-agent setup:

1. **Give the drafting agent the same read-only filesystem tools the planning agent has** (Read, Grep, Glob). Drafting without code visibility is what produces the \"trivial question\" failure mode. The agent should be able to answer its own questions about call sites, API shape, test layout etc. before grilling the user.

2. **Resolve the anvil path from the bead's anvil association** rather than asking. The Beads-Forge page already has the anvil selected; the daemon already knows `anvils.<name>.path` from config. The drafter's system prompt should be fed the resolved absolute path (or have a tool that returns it given the anvil name) so it never needs to ask.
design:
Likely touch points (verify before editing):
- `internal/web/forge_chat.go` or whatever assembles the drafting agent's system prompt + tool list — current version probably excludes Read/Grep/Glob.
- The chat-runner spawn path (forge_chat / forge_sessions) — pass the anvil's absolute path into the prompt as a fixed context line: \"You are drafting a bead for the `munin` anvil at `/home/forge/anvils/fhi.metadata`. Use Read/Grep against that path freely.\"
- The page-state on the React side already carries the anvil name (it's how the bead gets routed). No frontend change required if the backend resolves the path itself.
acceptance_criteria:
- Drafting a new bead for an anvil where the path is configured no longer asks the user for the path.
- The drafter can run Read/Grep/Glob against the anvil tree during the drafting conversation, without being explicitly told to "move to plan" first.
- A drafting session for a small dependency upgrade no longer produces a list of pre-questions whose answers are visible in the repo.
- The agent's system prompt verifiably includes the resolved anvil path (a quick \"what anvil path are you working with?\" probe returns the real value, not a request to provide one).
notes: Discovered today during a react-day-picker v9→v10 drafting session on the munin anvil. The 4 over-split beads that came out of that session (Fhi.Metadata-lenyo, -xmrma, -5hziz, -2kogb) were closed and replaced with one consolidated bead Fhi.Metadata-fel9j — see also the separate Beads-Forge over-splitting bead for the prompt tuning that produced the chain.

title: Temper dist-freshness check should also reject committed conflict markers in dist/
description:
## Problem

Forge-lmxc / PR #580 added a temper step that re-runs `npm run build` and fails when the resulting dist matches the committed dist (catching the "Smith changed frontend src but forgot to rerun the bundler" case). That check happens via `git status --porcelain -- internal/web/dist` after a clean rebuild — it only fires when the rebuild *would* change the file.

It does **not** fire when the committed dist file itself contains git merge-conflict markers (`<<<<<<<`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>`). If the rebuilt output happens to also contain markers in the same byte ranges (or if `npm run build` is skipped because the Paths filter didn't match), `git status` reports a clean tree and temper passes.

This bit production on 2026-05-11: skybert-forge's rebase Smith resolved a dist-bundle conflict during a rebase by leaving the markers in `internal/web/dist/assets/index-BdlG5RPS.js`, force-pushed the rebased branch, and the resulting PR (#599, commit 3dae39f3) merged cleanly. Local-forge then pulled the change and shipped the broken bundle. The pod started up healthy, served the HTML root fine, but every browser request for the JS asset got a 200 with a body that began:

    <<<<<<<< HEAD:internal/web/dist/assets/index-BdlG5RPS.js
    (function(){...

The SPA never executed (Chrome: `Uncaught SyntaxError: Unexpected token '<<'`) and Hearth 2.0 wouldn't render. Daemon was fine — only the embedded UI was broken.

## Proposed fix

Add a `VerifyNoConflictMarkers` mode to temper steps (or piggy-back on the existing embedded-bundle step) that greps the configured paths for the three marker patterns and fails the step when any are present. Cheap: ripgrep / git grep across `internal/web/dist/**` takes well under a second. Independent of the rebuild — runs even when the Paths filter would otherwise skip the npm install + build steps.

Gate it on the same path set as the existing freshness check so it stays self-contained to the hearth embedded-bundle layout.
design:
Two reasonable shapes:

**A. New temper field `VerifyNoConflictMarkers []string`** mirroring `VerifyClean` semantics — a list of pathspecs to grep after the step runs. Failure message names the offending file and the offending pattern. Auto-detected for the hearth embedded-bundle layout in `internal/temper/temper.go:embeddedBundleLayouts` so no per-anvil config change is needed.

**B. Roll the grep into the existing `hearth-frontend-build` step's post-condition** — when the step exits 0, run `git grep -lE '^(<{7}|={7}|>{7})' -- internal/web/dist/` and surface a failure if it returns any path. Slightly less general but keeps the surface area smaller.

A is the right shape long-term (other anvils that ship committed artefacts can opt in). Either works for the immediate case.

Do NOT scan the whole worktree — the markers are valid content inside markdown docs, prompts, test fixtures, etc. Only scan the *committed-artefact* paths that downstream code consumes verbatim (`internal/web/dist/**` today).
acceptance_criteria:
- A dist file containing any of `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>` (line-anchored, 7+ chars) makes temper fail with a clear message naming the file and the pattern.
- Step still passes when the markers appear inside markdown / prompt / fixture files outside the configured pathspecs.
- Unit tests cover: (a) clean dist passes, (b) `<<<<<<<` in a `.js` file fails, (c) markers in a docs file outside the pathspec are ignored.
- Auto-detection on the hearth embedded-bundle layout is on by default — no anvil config change required.
notes: Hit in production 2026-05-11 on commit 3dae39f3 (PR #599, Forge-48y4). The hetzner-forge rebase Smith left literal merge markers in `internal/web/dist/assets/index-BdlG5RPS.js`; the file shipped via the next `update-skybert.ps1` rollout. Web UI returned `Uncaught SyntaxError: Unexpected token '<<'` for every visitor until a manual `npm run build` rebuilt the bundle and a fresh image was pushed.

title: Daemon pidfile check should verify process identity, not just PID liveness
description:
## Problem

When a Forge pod is killed before `shutdown.Run()` gets a chance to clean up — failed helm rollout that scales the old pod down mid-flight, OOM kill, node drain exceeding the termination grace period — the `forge.pid` file at `/home/forge/.forge/forge.pid` is left behind on the PVC. The next pod to mount the PVC crashloops forever with `Forge daemon already running (PID 7)` before the daemon has even started. Recovery requires scaling to zero, mounting the PVC in a debug pod, deleting the pidfile, and scaling back up.

## Root cause

`internal/daemon/daemon.go:IsRunning` reads the pidfile, then checks liveness with `proc.Signal(0)` on Unix. In a fresh container PID namespace there is almost always *something* alive at low PIDs (container PID 1, init children, etc.), so the stale PID matches a live but unrelated process and the check returns `true`. The check has no way of knowing the running process is in fact a different Forge instance. The Windows path uses the named pipe as a liveness proxy and is unaffected — this is Linux-only.

## Proposed fix

Verify process identity, not just liveness. On Linux read `/proc/<pid>/comm` (or `/proc/<pid>/exe` for stronger identity) and check the basename matches `forge`. If the PID exists but is not a forge process, treat it as a stale pidfile: warn and continue startup as if the file weren't there.
design:
Linux-only change in `internal/daemon/daemon.go:IsRunning`. After `proc.Signal(0)` succeeds, additionally `os.Readlink("/proc/"+pid+"/exe")` (or read `/proc/<pid>/comm`) and compare the basename to `forge`. Mismatch → log warn, return `(0, false)` so startup proceeds and overwrites the pidfile.

Windows path already correctly verifies via the named pipe (which only exists if the daemon is actually running). Leave it alone.

No cross-container coordination is in scope — the pidfile is intentionally PVC-local; this is just about not tripping over its own ghost.
acceptance_criteria:
- Stale pidfile from force-kill no longer blocks startup when the PID is dead OR alive-but-not-a-forge-process.
- A genuinely-running second daemon (same binary on the same PVC) is still detected and rejected.
- Unit test on Linux covers: (a) dead PID, (b) live PID belonging to a forge process, (c) live PID belonging to some other process.
- Windows behaviour is unchanged.
notes: Hit in production 2026-05-11 during a skybert helm upgrade: new image tag didn't exist, deployment had already scaled down the old pod, every retry pod crashlooped because PID 7 in their PID namespace was something else but pidfile said "7 means forge".

title: Wire per-PR actions via IPC and gh CLI
description: Implement action handlers on each PR row: merge, assign-bellows (MANUAL only — button click, no auto-assign; add a comment noting reliance on Forge-i1g7 per-instance ownership), approve, fix-comments (burnish), fix-ci (quench), fix-conflicts (rebase), reset-counters, close. For forge_prs and recently_merged: dispatch via in-process IPC to the daemon's existing pr_action handler (reuse Hytte's IPC client from PRModal.tsx). For external_prs: approve and merge call `gh pr review --approve` and `gh pr merge` directly; other actions remain IPC-routed where applicable or are hidden for external PRs. Add per-action loading/error states. Depends on sub-tasks 1 (UI rows) and 2 (PR identity from data sources).

title: Add /prs tab scaffolding and AppHeader integration
description: Create web/src/components/hearth/PRsTab.tsx as a new tab component (not a modal), structured after web/src/components/mezzanine/PRModal.tsx but adapted to tab layout. Wire into AppHeader's tab registry/router so /prs route renders it. Define the three section containers (forge_prs, external_prs, recently_merged) with empty states and section headers. Establish shared types (PRItem, PRSection) in a colocated types file. This sub-task lays the UI shell that the data-fetching and action sub-tasks plug into.

title: Implement PR data sources (forge, external, recently_merged)
description: Add data hooks: useForgePRs() reads from state.db (reuse existing daemon state query used by Hytte's PRModal); useExternalPRs() shells out to `gh pr list` filtered to other contributors, with a 60-second in-memory cache (timestamp + invalidation on manual refresh); useRecentlyMergedPRs() fetches merged PRs from the same backend. Place in web/src/components/hearth/usePRsData.ts. Sub-task 1 consumes these hooks to render section contents. Ensure cache key includes repo identity to avoid cross-repo bleed.

title: Hearth 2.0: Beads-Forge page — multi-bead emission with dep graph + anvil routing
description: Third and final bead in the Beads-Forge feature. Once a session is in stage=agreed, the user clicks 'Create Bead(s)' and claude emits a structured list of 1..N beads (each with target anvil, title, description, type, priority, labels, depends_on) which the backend materialises by shelling out to bd in the right anvil's directory and wiring deps. Atomic: if any bd create fails partway, the previously-created beads are rolled back via bd close --reason='rollback: parent create failed'.
design: Finalisation prompt requires claude to honour the session anvil unless explicitly multi-anvil — otherwise it routes one-per-default. Each bead's description should embed a footer 'Created via Beads-Forge session #<id>' for traceability and auditing. Labels: include 'forgeReady' by default unless the session-level labels say otherwise; user can edit labels per-bead in the preview before commit (post-MVP — not in scope here). The bd subprocess invocation must use --description= rather than stdin to avoid shell-quoting hazards on multi-line descriptions; if too long for a single arg, write to a temp file and use --description-file (verify bd supports this; if not, use printf and a here-doc). Don't auto-tag forgeReady on beads in the Forge anvil unless target=Forge — for skybert-forge users, beads in heimdall/munin should default to forgeReady but Forge anvil should be left unlabelled (so user manually decides which forge gets it). Frontend: new <CreateBeadsView> renders the proposed bead list returned by claude with each bead's anvil/title/desc/labels/deps; user gets one final review before pressing the button. Display real-time progress as each bd create lands (SSE or simple polled status).
acceptance_criteria: (1) Backend handler POST /api/forge/sessions/{id}/create-beads: requires stage=agreed. Spawns claude one final time with a 'finalisation' system prompt that asks for JSON {beads: [{title, description, anvil, type, priority, labels: [], depends_on: []}, ...]}. Validates schema. (2) For each bead in order: cd /home/forge/anvils/<anvil> && bd create --title=... --description=... --type=... --priority=... [+ labels via bd tag]. Capture the resulting bead ID from stdout (regex on '✓ Created issue: <ID>'). Store in a session_beads (session_id, bead_id, anvil, created_at) join table. (3) After all beads created, walk the depends_on edges: bd dep add <bead> <depends-on>. (4) On any bd create or dep add error: rollback. Iterate previously-created beads in reverse order calling 'bd close <id> --reason="rollback: bead-forge session N create-beads failed at step M"'. Surface the original error to the user via a clear toast + a system message in the conversation. (5) On success: session stage transitions to 'created'. Frontend shows the bead list with links into the existing Hearth 2.0 /bead/<id> detail page. Display the dep graph as a simple ASCII or visual tree. (6) Idempotency: re-clicking 'Create Bead(s)' on a created session is a no-op (returns the existing bead list). To re-emit, user must explicitly create a new session.
notes: Builds on Forge-ljv5. Edge cases: (a) cycles in depends_on — validate up front, refuse to create. (b) Bead in anvil X depending on bead in anvil Y — bd may not support cross-anvil deps; verify and document or refuse. (c) Subprocess must inherit the same environment as smith spawning so bd connects to dolt correctly. (d) Cost: this final claude turn is small (just emit JSON); track but don't enforce. Long-term: post-MVP polish includes editing the proposed bead list before commit, dragging dep edges visually, retry on partial-fail, etc. Out of scope for v1.

title: Hearth 2.0: Beads-Forge page — claude integration, plan, grilling stage
description: Second of three beads. Builds on the UI skeleton from Forge-qcqv to add the actual AI flow: claude is spawned per-turn to advance the conversation, the user can request a plan, and the page enters a grilling stage where claude exhausts the decision tree by emitting structured questions. The grill-me skill prompt (per user instructions) is baked into the system message during grilling. Each stage has a different system prompt and different UI affordances.
design: System prompts live in internal/forge_design/prompts.go: planSystemPrompt (asks for a markdown plan with specific sections: Problem/Goal/Approach/Risks/Open questions); grillSystemPrompt (the grill-me skill text from the user, plus 'output JSON in this exact shape: {questions: [...]}'). Claude invocation: build a single user message that concatenates [system prompt, all conversation messages, plan-so-far, request-for-this-turn]. Use --output-format=json so we get a deterministic envelope including total_cost_usd. Parse the assistant's content as either markdown (planning) or JSON (grilling). Validate JSON schema before persistence; on invalid, treat as grilling-failed and add a system note 'claude returned invalid JSON, retry'. Stage transitions are server-authoritative — frontend triggers transition via API call, backend validates current stage and writes new stage atomically. Idempotency: re-calling /plan from drafting works; from planning replaces the latest plan. Auto-transition planning -> grilling happens at end of /plan handler if plan parsing succeeded. Anvil routing: a new field forge_sessions.target_anvil set during /plan from claude's structured output (claude is asked which anvil based on conversation context); user can override via PATCH /api/forge/sessions/{id} with {anvil: ...}.
acceptance_criteria: (1) Spawning: new internal/forge_design/runner.go that invokes 'claude -p --output-format=json' subprocess, piping in conversation history as a structured prompt, capturing stdout + stderr + cost. CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN inherited from env. Per-turn timeout 5 min. (2) Stage state machine: drafting -> planning -> grilling -> agreed (with rejected off-ramp from any stage). Backend transition handlers: POST /api/forge/sessions/{id}/plan (drafting -> planning, runs claude with plan-system-prompt, stores plan as new assistant message + sets stage to planning, then auto-transitions to grilling and runs claude with grill-me-system-prompt). POST /api/forge/sessions/{id}/grill-respond accepts user answers and re-spawns claude to continue. POST /api/forge/sessions/{id}/agree (grilling -> agreed). (3) Grilling output format: claude is instructed to emit JSON {questions: [{id, question, options: [], recommendation, status: 'open'|'answered', answer?}]}. Backend parses; on parse error, retries once, then falls back to free-text in the conversation. (4) Frontend: new <GrillPanel> component renders Q&A list. Each unanswered question shows options (clickable buttons), the recommendation pre-highlighted, plus a free-text input. Picking an option or submitting text appends to the messages array and POSTs to grill-respond. When all questions are 'answered', shows an 'Agree and proceed to bead creation' button. (5) Plan rendering: when stage=planning|grilling|agreed, the latest plan is shown above the conversation in a sticky <PlanView> with markdown rendering. (6) Cost tracking per turn: cost_usd written on each assistant message; daily total visible in session header. No enforcement — track only (subscription mode).
notes: Builds on Forge-qcqv. Skill prompt to embed: 'Interview me relentlessly about every aspect of this plan until we reach a shared understanding. Walk down each branch of the design tree resolving dependencies between decisions one by one. If a question can be answered by exploring the codebase, explore the codebase instead. For each question, provide your recommended answer.' Plus 'questions should have options and recommendation(s); user responds by either writing or picking an option'. Multi-bead structure (claude proposes 1..N beads with deps) is the next bead's concern (Forge-bf-create); this bead delivers a single agreed-upon plan that's ready to be turned into beads.

title: Hearth 2.0: Beads-Forge page — UI skeleton, conversation persistence, draft input
description: First of three beads delivering a Hytte-Suggestions-style page in Hearth 2.0 for iteratively designing beads through conversation with claude. This bead delivers ONLY the foundation: a new /forge route (or /design — pick name during impl) with: a session list sidebar, a chat-style conversation view, a free-text 'new session' draft input, and the persistence layer. No claude integration yet (next bead handles that), no grilling yet (third bead). Scope is intentionally narrow so the layer can be reviewed in isolation.
design: Tables: forge_sessions has columns id INTEGER PK, user TEXT, title TEXT, anvil TEXT (nullable, set later), stage TEXT, created_at TIMESTAMP, updated_at TIMESTAMP. forge_messages has id INTEGER PK, session_id INTEGER FK, role TEXT (user|assistant|system), content TEXT, ts TIMESTAMP, plus optional cost_usd REAL for later token accounting. Index on (user, updated_at DESC) for fast list. No encryption — skybert single-tenant, PVC + login auth is enough. Stage transitions allowed in this bead: drafting -> rejected (via DELETE) only; further transitions handled by next beads. Frontend tabs uses react-router /forge/ and /forge/new for routing into a session. Reuse the existing apiGet/apiPost helpers; fetch session list once on mount + after each create. Conversation rendering: simple <Message> component with role-styled bubbles (slate-800 for assistant, amber-tinted for user — match Hearth 2.0's palette). Auto-scroll to bottom on new message.
acceptance_criteria: (1) New /forge route in App.tsx + nav link in AppHeader.tsx (after Costs). (2) Backend: new state.db tables forge_sessions (id, user, title, anvil, stage, created_at, updated_at) and forge_messages (id, session_id, role, content, ts) with migrations in internal/state/db.go. Stage enum: drafting | planning | grilling | agreed | created | rejected. (3) Backend handlers in new internal/web/views_forge.go: GET /api/forge/sessions (list user's sessions), GET /api/forge/sessions/{id} (full session + messages), POST /api/forge/sessions (create new draft from user's first message body — returns id), POST /api/forge/sessions/{id}/messages (append a user message), DELETE /api/forge/sessions/{id} (soft-delete via stage=rejected). All require auth + csrf; user_id scoping on read/write. (4) Frontend page ForgePage.tsx with three columns: session list, conversation thread (assistant on left, user on right, ts shown), input box at bottom with Send button. Stage indicator at top. (5) Empty state: 'Start a new session' with a textarea and Create button. (6) NO claude calls yet — sessions stay in 'drafting' indefinitely; the input adds messages but doesn't trigger any AI. Reviewable as a static thread.
notes: Foundation bead — no AI integration. Next beads: Forge-bf-grill (claude integration + plan + grilling stage), Forge-bf-create (multi-bead emission). Reference Hytte's pages/Suggestions.tsx for high-level page layout patterns. Skip auto-suggestion generator (Hytte's nightly cron) for v1 — defer to v2; if it's added later, page-scoped context for munin/heimdall would be the integration point.

title: Hearth 2.0: PRs tab — full PR triage panel mirroring Hytte mezzanine
description: Add a /prs tab to Hearth 2.0 that mirrors Hytte's PR shortcut panel (web/src/components/mezzanine/PRModal.tsx) — but as a tab in AppHeader, not a modal. Lists three sections: forge_prs (Forge-created, from state.db), external_prs (other contributors' PRs via gh pr list, cached 60s), recently_merged. Per-PR actions: merge, assign-bellows, approve, fix-comments (burnish), fix-ci (quench), fix-conflicts (rebase), reset-counters, close. External PR approve/merge call gh CLI directly; everything else dispatches via in-process IPC to the daemon's existing pr_action handler. The bellows assignment must be MANUAL (user clicks button) — relies on Forge-i1g7's per-instance ownership for safety once that lands; prior to i1g7 a manually-assigned PR could still be fought over by another forge, but that's the user's choice and matches existing Hytte semantics.
design: Frontend modeled on Hytte's PRModal.tsx but laid out as a tab page: collapsible sections per anvil within each list (forge / external / merged), action buttons inline. Reuse ConfirmModal + useToast + useAction. Types lifted from Hytte's useAllPRs.ts: OpenPR, ExternalPR, MergedPR. Backend mirrors Hytte's handlers in internal/api/handlers.go but uses Forge's daemon IPC directly (Hytte calls forge daemon over a socket; we have it in-process). External PR fetch uses gh pr list --state=open --json ... --search '-author:forge-skybert' or similar to avoid double-listing forge-created ones. Cache the gh result for 60s in-memory (sync.Map keyed by anvil). For external bellows-assignment, daemon already has IPC command 'pr_action' with action='assign_bellows' — extend if needed but likely works. Anvil grouping: client-side groupBy on .anvil after the API returns flat lists. SSE filtering: subscribe to /api/activity/stream and filter event type for pr_* (ci_passed, ci_failed, review_approved, etc); refetch the relevant section on each match.
acceptance_criteria: (1) New /prs route in App.tsx + nav link in AppHeader.tsx between History and Costs. (2) Backend handlers in internal/web/views_prs.go (GET /api/prs/all returns {forge, external, recently_merged}) and internal/web/actions_prs.go (POST /api/prs/{id}/{merge|bellows|approve|fix-comments|fix-ci|fix-conflicts|reset-counters|close} for forge PRs and POST /api/ext-prs/{action} for external PRs taking {repo, number}). (3) Frontend page PRsPage.tsx renders three collapsible anvil-grouped sections, status badges (CIBadge, ReviewBadge mirrored from Hytte), confirm modal on every action via existing ConfirmModal, optimistic disable while in flight, toast on success/error. (4) Live updates via existing /api/activity/stream SSE filtered to pr_* event types — no separate poller, no 30s timer. (5) All POST endpoints behind requireAuth + csrfCheck; frontend uses apiPost so X-Forge-Action is set. (6) Action set conditionally rendered: Fix CI only when ci_passing=false, Fix Conflicts only when is_conflicting=true, etc. (7) Empty states for each section with zero PRs.
notes: Reference: Hytte web/src/components/mezzanine/PRModal.tsx (697 lines, anvil grouping + 7 action buttons with confirm dialogs); Hytte internal/api/handlers.go MergePRHandler/BellowsPRHandler/etc; Hytte web/src/hooks/useAllPRs.ts (TypeScript types). Bellows safety: this feature lists all PRs but bellows-assignment is manual + per-PR. Auto-adoption (the bug we just hit) is a separate concern fixed by Forge-i1g7. No keyboard shortcut for v1 (tab nav is enough).
close_reason: Decomposed into 3 sub-beads: Forge-6321, Forge-9ye8, Forge-x7dy

title: Forge: orphan-recovery loops on a closed bead with an open PR
description: When a bead is closed externally (via 'bd close' from a teammate's machine) while forge has it tracked as in_progress in its in-memory or state.db tracking, forge's orphan-recovery loop keeps resetting the bead's status back to open and re-dispatching it — even though the corresponding PR is already open and the work is done. This was hit during the skybert cutover (2026-05-08) on Heimdall-tgmp and required a pod restart + tag removal to break the loop. The redispatch dance also produces noisy 'no changes needed' smith iterations that cost tokens.
design: Two failure modes to handle: (1) the bead's status drifts to in_progress in forge's local view but the remote dolt has it closed (sync race); (2) forge has a local retry record marking the bead as in-flight but no actual smith worker exists. Both should be cured by an early-out in the recovery path that calls 'gh pr list --head forge/<bead-id> --state=open --json number' and short-circuits when a PR exists. Bonus: when an open PR is detected, forge should call 'bd close <bead-id> --reason="PR #N created"' to harmonise the state across the team.
acceptance_criteria: When forge detects an orphaned in_progress bead, the recovery decision tree must check: (a) is the corresponding remote forge/<bead-id> branch present? (b) is there an open PR pointing at it? If yes to both, the recovery should skip the status-reset and instead let bellows continue monitoring the PR — the bead should be left in a 'pending-merge' state (or simply closed with a note) rather than re-dispatched. Eliminate the case where the same bead is dispatched twice in a row with smith returning 'no changes needed' both times.
notes: Discovered on skybert deploy of Hearth 2.0 (2026-05-08). Heimdall-tgmp ended up creating PR #255 (FHIDev/Heimdall) but then forge looped through 4–5 redispatch cycles with smith spending tokens to declare 'no work needed' each time. Fix unblocks reliable end-to-end deps-update flow.

title: Hearth 2.0: /login should redirect to / when already authenticated
description: When a user is already authenticated and navigates to https://forge.skytest.fhi.no/login, they're shown the login form instead of being redirected to the dashboard. The login form is still functional (you can log in again, even if redundant), but the right behaviour is: if the session cookie is valid, /login should immediately redirect to /. The frontend already has a /api/auth/status (or equivalent) check that handlers.go's handleLoginStatus exposes — the login page should call that on mount and redirect if authenticated:true.
design: Easiest fix is in the React LoginPage component (internal/web/frontend/src/pages/LoginPage.tsx): on mount, fire GET /api/auth/login-status (or the existing equivalent endpoint); if response says authenticated:true, navigate('/'). Show a small spinner during the auth-status check to avoid flashing the form for already-logged-in users.
acceptance_criteria: Logged-in user navigating to /login is redirected to / within one render cycle (no flicker of the login form). Unauthenticated user navigating to /login still sees the login form. Logging out from / and re-visiting /login still shows the form. No regressions to the existing login flow.
notes: Discovered during skybert cutover (2026-05-08). Reachable example: deployed Hearth 2.0 at https://forge.skytest.fhi.no/login while having a valid session cookie.
